An apriori power calculation was conducted using a small effect size (d = 0.15) and revealed that n = 111 participants were needed to achieve 95% statistical power using the standard 0.05 alpha value.

Participants were presented with five different technologies with the largest difference in affect ratings for positive and negative images (electric air travel, biomass energy production, small modular reactors, self-driving taxis, and hydropower energy production) in a randomized block-wise order along with a short description of what the technology is and how it works.
For each technology, participants were randomly assigned to either a positive or a negative block.
As such, participants were not divided into positive and negative manipulation groups but had an equal probability to view either negative or positive images of any given technology.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 80 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (80). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Seventy-seven human participants aged 19-79 years old (M = 39.61, SD = 14.53) from the United States were recruited via prolific (www.prolific.com), 48 of which identified as female, 28 identified as male, and one identified as non-binary.
All participants received monetary compensation amounting to £12/hour for their involvement in accordance with Prolific fair pay guidelines and institutional ethical standards.
Participants were informed of the purpose, aims, and the potential risks and benefits of the study when giving informed consent.
Participants were presented with 13 different technologies in a randomized order (Table S1).

To measure affect, participants were asked to indicate how positive or negative they felt about the technologies on a nine-point Likert scale (1 = extremely negative,9 = extremely positive) with the prompt "How do you feel about [technology]?".

Given the nested repeated-measure nature of the data in which participants provided multiple ratings across different technologies and targets, a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) approach was appropriate to test both hypotheses.
One-hundred-fifty participants aged 18-79 years old (M = 40.99, SD = 13.61) from the United States were recruited via prolific (www.prolific.com).

The inclusion criteria were identical to Study 1, and all participants received monetary compensation amounting to £13.69/hour for their involvement in accordance with Prolific fair pay guidelines and institutional ethical standards.

An apriori power calculation was conducted using a small effect size (d = 0.15) and revealed that n = 111 participants were needed to achieve 95% statistical power using the standard 0.05 alpha value.

Participants were presented with five different technologies with the largest difference in affect ratings for positive and negative images (electric air travel, biomass energy production, small modular reactors, self-driving taxis, and hydropower energy production) in a randomized block-wise order along with a short description of what the technology is and how it works.
For each technology, participants were randomly assigned to either a positive or a negative block.
As such, participants were not divided into positive and negative manipulation groups but had an equal probability to view either negative or positive images of any given technology.

text.text: Affective evaluations play a central role in risk perception, yet it remains unclear whether affect shapes judgments differently when risks are evaluated for oneself versus others.
Across two studies, we tested whether hazard-directed affect exerts a differential influence on self-focused and other-focused risk judgments.

Study 1 (N = 77) featured a repeated-measures design in which participants rated affect, perceived risk, and perceived benefit for 13 technologies for themselves and for a random other, allowing within-person comparisons of self-and otherfocused judgments.

A linear mixed-effects model indicated that although negative affect predicted higher perceived risk and positive affect predicted lower perceived risk, the influence of affect did not differ across judgment targets.
With the same design, Study 2 (N = 150) experimentally manipulated hazard-directed affect using negatively versus positively valenced images across five technologies.
The positive affect manipulation lowered perceived risk while negative affect increased perceived risk.
The influence of the manipulation did not differ across judgment targets.

Additionally, we examined whether the inverse association between perceived risk and perceived benefit, an indicator of the affect heuristic, varied by target: evidence for a stronger inverse association for other-focused judgments emerged in Study 1, suggesting affective cues may be relied upon more readily when making judgements for others.
This finding did not replicate in Study 2.

Together, our findings refine affect-based accounts of risk perception by suggesting affective evaluations of hazards are applied similarly across judgment targets, even when self-other differences in risk level are present.
Judgments of risk are strongly shaped by affective reactions.

Alongside deliberative "risk-asanalysis" processes, people often draw on "risk-as-feelings," where experienced feelings provide rapid information about how risky a hazard seems (Loewenstein et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Alongside deliberative "risk-asanalysis" processes, people often draw on "risk-as-feelings," where experienced feelings provide rapid information about how risky a hazard seems <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Loewenstein et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In this tradition, affect refers to an evaluative reaction to a stimulus, experienced as its perceived "goodness" or "badness", and can guide judgments even when people have limited knowledge or when decisions are complex (Slovic et al., 2004).
text.formatted: In this tradition, affect refers to an evaluative reaction to a stimulus, experienced as its perceived "goodness" or "badness", and can guide judgments even when people have limited knowledge or when decisions are complex <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Slovic et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Separable from deliberate and experiential components, contemporary models treat affective influences as a distinct ingredient in risk perception (Ferrer et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Separable from deliberate and experiential components, contemporary models treat affective influences as a distinct ingredient in risk perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Ferrer et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, risk perception is not merely calculation; it is also an affectively infused judgment about potential harm.

A core framework for this idea is the affect heuristic, which proposes that people, instead of rationally reflecting on risks and benefits separately, use their immediate affective evaluation as a cue when judging both risks and benefits (Finucane et al., 2000; Slovic et al., 2007).

text.text: When a hazard elicits positive affect, it tends to be judged as more beneficial and less risky; when it elicits negative affect, it tends to be judged as less beneficial and more risky (Alhakami & Slovic, 1994; Finucane et al., 2000).
text.formatted: When a hazard elicits positive affect, it tends to be judged as more beneficial and less risky; when it elicits negative affect, it tends to be judged as less beneficial and more risky <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alhakami & Slovic, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Finucane et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: While societies seem to accept higher risks for more beneficial activities (Starr, 1969), people perceive that beneficial activities are less risky (Fischhoff et al., 1978; Slovic et al., 2004).

text.text: As argued by Slovic et al. (2004), because high risks are generally only societally accepted if their benefits are also high, a rational hazarddirected risk and benefit judgment of societal risks (e.g., nuclear energy, vaccines, hydroelectric dams, high-speed rail networks) ought to be positively correlated.

(2004)</ref>, because high risks are generally only societally accepted if their benefits are also high, a rational hazarddirected risk and benefit judgment of societal risks (e.g., nuclear energy, vaccines, hydroelectric dams, high-speed rail networks) ought to be positively correlated.

text.text: The inverse perceived risk-benefit association is thus commonly interpreted as an indicator of an affectbased heuristic being relied upon in decision-making.

Supporting this interpretation, Skagerlund et al. (2020) finds this association largely stable across elicitation methods and domains of risk, although its strength varied with individual differences in cognitive reflection abilities.

text.text: This inverse correlation between perceived risks and benefits has been replicated (Efendić et al., 2021) and expanded upon (Skagerlund et al., 2020) in studies within the affect heuristic literature.

text.text: Recent experimental work in risk communication research shows affective cues can shape perceived risk: Keller et al. (2006) found that participants exposed to images of flooded houses perceived greater flood risks compared to controls.

text.text: Complementing this experimental evidence, Västfjäll et al. (2014) showed that incidental negative affect following a natural disaster was associated with higher perceived risks and stronger risk-benefit associations, although this effect varied across domains.

(2014)</ref> showed that incidental negative affect following a natural disaster was associated with higher perceived risks and stronger risk-benefit associations, although this effect varied across domains.

text.text: Together, this literature indicates affective evaluations, whether measured directly or induced through contextual cues, systematically shape judgments of perceived risk and perceived benefit.
Importantly, risk judgments are not only made for oneself, but also for other people.
A broad literature on self-other decision-making suggests judgments and choices for others often diverge from those made for oneself, although this finding is not uniform across different contexts.

Rather, meta-analyses suggest self-other differences in decision-making are domaindependent, with no consistent tendency for people to make either more or less risky choices for themselves compared to others (Batteux et al., 2019).

text.text: Whereas Batteux et al. (2019) work finds no consistent directional self-other discrepancy, this work primarily examined the self-other differences within risky choice paradigms and not the perceived risk level of specific hazards depending on judgment target.

(2019)</ref> work finds no consistent directional self-other discrepancy, this work primarily examined the self-other differences within risky choice paradigms and not the perceived risk level of specific hazards depending on judgment target.

text.text: Looking beyond risky choice paradigms, self-other distinctions appear in judgments of vulnerability, safety, and health (Stone et al., 2013; Yeater et al., 2009).

text.text: Crucially, self-other differences are observed when people judge both risks and benefits.
In the case of smoking, smokers perceived greater benefits and lower risks pertaining to smoking for themselves when compared to other smokers (Zlatev et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In the case of smoking, smokers perceived greater benefits and lower risks pertaining to smoking for themselves when compared to other smokers <ref type="bibr">(Zlatev et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern, in which people perceive their own risk as lower compared to the risks faced by others, is commonly labeled as unrealistic optimism or a self-other discrepancy (Shepperd et al., 2013; Weinstein, 1989) and recent meta-analytic evidence suggests this is reflected in climate-related risk perceptions across datasets and countries (Sandlund et al., 2026).

text.text: Further, Sandlund et al. (2026) demonstrates this gap between self and other increases as the judgment target becomes more general (e.g., the average person in your country) as compared to more specific (e.g. your neighbor).

text.text: Thus, prior work shows that self-and other-focused risk judgments often diverge, especially when the "other" is more abstract or socially distant.
Taken together, prior work suggests that affective cues shape judgments of risks and benefits and that risk perceptions differ depending on whether they concern the self or another person.
What remains unclear is whether affective cues are weighted differently across these types of judgments.
Existing theory suggests two competing possibilities.
One possibility is that affective evaluations exert a weaker influence when people judge risks for others.
Risk-asfeelings accounts emphasize that affective influences are strongest when outcomes are vivid and personally experienced (Loewenstein et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Risk-asfeelings accounts emphasize that affective influences are strongest when outcomes are vivid and personally experienced <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Loewenstein et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Judgments about personal risks may therefore provide the most experientially rich reference point, whereas judgments about others hinge more on deliberate or analytical processing.

This line of argument aligns with research showing that self-other differences in risky choices increase in magnitude as the target of the judgment becomes more general or psychologically distant (Hsee & Weber, 1997).
text.formatted: This line of argument aligns with research showing that self-other differences in risky choices increase in magnitude as the target of the judgment becomes more general or psychologically distant <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hsee & Weber, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, this account is consistent with work on hot-cold empathy gaps and predictions of others' risky preferences, suggesting that individuals underestimate the influence of affective states when these states are not personally experienced, leading to more deliberate or analytically mediated rather than affective judgments about others (Faro & Rottenstreich, 2006; Loewenstein, 1996).
text.formatted: Relatedly, this account is consistent with work on hot-cold empathy gaps and predictions of others' risky preferences, suggesting that individuals underestimate the influence of affective states when these states are not personally experienced, leading to more deliberate or analytically mediated rather than affective judgments about others <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Faro & Rottenstreich, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Loewenstein, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: A different line of thinking follows classic affect-as-information accounts.

When people judge risks for general or underspecified others, a lack of concrete individuating information about judgment targets may make one's feelings about the hazard itself more accessible (Schwarz & Clore, 1983 , 2003).
text.formatted: When people judge risks for general or underspecified others, a lack of concrete individuating information about judgment targets may make one's feelings about the hazard itself more accessible <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Schwarz & Clore, 1983</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, hazard-directed affect need not be attenuated by psychological distance or abstraction; it may instead be applied similarly across judgment targets.

A stronger interpretation would imply that because hazard-directed affect can serve as a general cue for decision-making, underspecified or low-information targets may increase reliance on affective cues when less information is available for deliberate risk assessment (Finucane et al., 2000; Slovic et al., 2007).
text.formatted: A stronger interpretation would imply that because hazard-directed affect can serve as a general cue for decision-making, underspecified or low-information targets may increase reliance on affective cues when less information is available for deliberate risk assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Finucane et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Slovic et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Prior work within risky choice paradigms has largely examined choices pertaining to the risk preferences of others, while affect-heuristic research has examined how affective cues influence the perception of risks and benefits.

Moreover, empathy-gap and risky-choice studies often concern the projection of one's own preferences or affective evaluation onto another person, rather than the influence of hazard-directed affect toward specific societal risks.

This gap in current knowledge, together with the competing theoretical accounts outlined above, leaves an unresolved question: Do affective evaluations shape perceived risk differently depending on whether the judgment is self-focused or other-focused?
Answering this question is theoretically relevant to understanding the role of affect in risk judgments concerning others.
It is also practically relevant in contexts where risk judgments about others inform policy interventions and risk communication (Slovic, 1987).
text.formatted: It is also practically relevant in contexts where risk judgments about others inform policy interventions and risk communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Slovic, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: To address this research question, we tested whether affective evaluations of hazards operate similarly across targets (self vs. other), and whether a key marker of affect-heuristic processing, the inverse relationship between perceived risk and perceived benefit, differs across targets.
Across two studies, participants evaluated technologies and provided perceived risk and benefit judgments for themselves and for another person (a random person in the United States).
Study 1 assessed self-reported affective evaluation of each technology; Study 2 experimentally manipulated affect via valenced imagery.

Given the theoretical ambiguity outlined above, we tested two non-directional hypotheses: (H1) affective influence on perceived risk differs as a function of target (self vs. other), and (H2) the inverse risk-benefit relationship differs as a function of target. a a The data were originally collected as part of a preregistered project addressing a different research question and aim.

text.text: Given the nested repeated-measure nature of the data in which participants provided multiple ratings across different technologies and targets, a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) approach was appropriate to test both hypotheses.

As there may be asymmetric effects of affect valence: for example, negative affect may steeply increase perceived risk, whereas positive affect may reduce risk judgments more gradually, we employed a piecewise (spline) LMM to account for the potentially distinct slopes for negative and positive affect rather than assuming a single linear relationship.

As such, the affect variable was split at the midpoint: Negative affect (values below the neutral midpoint, re-coded to reflect increasing negativity) and Positive affect (values above the midpoint, re-coded to reflect increasing positivity).
Perceived benefit was grand mean centered prior to analysis to increase interpretability and reduce potential multicollinearity issues.
All t-tests used Satterthwaite approximation with REML estimation.

text.text: Study 1 examined whether affective evaluations of hazards shape perceived risk differently depending on whether judgments are made for oneself or for another person.
Consistent with core predictions from the affect heuristic, both negative and positive affect strongly predicted perceived risk.

Interestingly, one standard deviation higher in negative affect toward the target hazard increased perceived risk by 0.26 standard deviation while one standard deviation higher positive affect reduced perceived risk with 0.39 standard deviation.
This emphasizes that risk assessment is not only driven by negative affect toward the hazard but also from positive affect.

This pattern aligns with extensive evidence that affect serves as an evaluative cue in judgments of both risk and benefit, often producing the characteristic inverse relationship between perceived risk and perceived benefit (Alhakami & Slovic, 1994; Finucane et al., 2000; Keller et al., 2006; Slovic et al., 2004 Slovic et al., , 2007)).
text.formatted: This pattern aligns with extensive evidence that affect serves as an evaluative cue in judgments of both risk and benefit, often producing the characteristic inverse relationship between perceived risk and perceived benefit <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alhakami & Slovic, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Finucane et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Keller et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Slovic et al., 2004</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Slovic et al., , 2007))</ref>.

text.text: Contrary to the prediction that affective influence should differ as a function of target (H1), affect did not interact with target: the affect-risk association was statistically comparable for self-and other-focused judgments.

This null interaction is theoretically informative because "risk-as-feelings" accounts are often interpreted to imply stronger affective influence when judgment targets are more concrete and experientially grounded (Loewenstein et al., 2001).

text.text: Similarly, research on self-other discrepancies in risky choice suggests that abstraction can reduce reliance on one's own feelings when predicting others (Hsee & Weber, 1997).

text.text: The present findings suggest that this general self>other expectation does not straightforwardly extend to contexts where affect is directed toward a shared hazard object.
text.formatted: The present findings suggest that this general self>other expectation does not straightforwardly extend to contexts where affect is directed toward a shared hazard object.

text.text: One interpretation is that when affect is an evaluation of the technology itself, it provides a general input that is readily applied to judgments for both self and other.

In addition to this target-invariant affect effect, Study 1 showed evidence for self-other differences in the risk-benefit association: the inverse relationship between perceived risk and perceived benefit was stronger for judgments made for others than for judgments made for oneself.
This pattern is consistent with the idea that judgments about unfamiliar others may sometimes show stronger reliance on heuristic signatures (Finucane et al., 2000; Slovic et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with the idea that judgments about unfamiliar others may sometimes show stronger reliance on heuristic signatures <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Finucane et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Slovic et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, this interaction persisted after controlling for self-reported affect, despite the main effect of perceived benefit becoming non-significant.

This suggests that while affective cues account for much of the overall inverse association between risk and benefit, we cannot conclusively say that the differences in the risk-benefit correlation are directly related to the affect heuristic.
In other words, the stronger risk-benefit coupling for others in Study 1 is not easily explained as simply "more affect" for other judgments.

Instead, it may reflect differences in how participants integrate information about benefits across targets, or differences in uncertainty about others that shift how benefit and risk judgments cohere.

Finally, an exploratory analysis suggested that self-other differences in perceived risk may have narrowed across the repeated sequence, consistent with potential fatigue or adaptation across repeated ratings.

Although this effect was weak and should be interpreted cautiously, it highlights a design consideration for repeated-measures risk perception tasks: extensive repetition may reduce target differentiation over time.

To account for this potential limitation and experimentally manipulate affective factors, we designed Study 2 aimed at reducing intensity and testing the causal relationship between affect and perceived risk.

Study 2 employed a 2 (Affect: positive & negative) x 2 (Target: self & other) x 5 (Technology: electric flying, small modular reactors, hydropower energy production, biomass energy production, self-driving taxi) mixed design with target, technology, and manipulation as within-subjects.

text.text: The outcome variable was perceived risk.
One-hundred-fifty participants aged 18-79 years old (M = 40.99, SD = 13.61) from the United States were recruited via prolific (www.prolific.com).

text.text: Out of these, 74 identified as female and 76 identified as male.
The average completion time for the survey was approximately eight minutes and data collection occurred on the 24th of April 2025 via Qualtrics (Qualtrics, 2025).

The inclusion criteria were identical to Study 1, and all participants received monetary compensation amounting to £13.69/hour for their involvement in accordance with Prolific fair pay guidelines and institutional ethical standards.
Participants were informed of the purpose, aims, and the potential risks and benefits of the study when giving informed consent.
The final sample size used in analysis was (n = 150) as all participants fully completed the survey.

An apriori power calculation was conducted using a small effect size (d = 0.15) and revealed that n = 111 participants were needed to achieve 95% statistical power using the standard 0.05 alpha value.
Drawing from previous methodology on affect manipulation (Efendić 2021; Keller et al., 2006), affect was manipulated through negatively and positively valenced images.

text.text: Images were generated through the large language model ChatGPT (OpenAI, GPT-4o, 2025) and pre-tested in a separate data-collection procedure where participants (n=75) rated how negatively or positively valenced these images were perceived on a Likert scale (1 = extremely negative to9 = extremely positive).

As the juxtaposition between negative and positive affect is paramount for contrasting conditions, technologies and images used as stimulus material were selected based on the difference in mean affect ratings for the most negative and most positive image pairs within each technology.
The resulting affective contrast between these pairs of images was substantial (d = 2.02).
For a detailed description of the pre-testing procedures, see section 3 in the supplementary materials.

Participants were presented with five different technologies with the largest difference in affect ratings for positive and negative images (electric air travel, biomass energy production, small modular reactors, self-driving taxis, and hydropower energy production) in a randomized block-wise order along with a short description of what the technology is and how it works.
For each technology, participants were randomly assigned to either a positive or a negative block.
As such, participants were not divided into positive and negative manipulation groups but had an equal probability to view either negative or positive images of any given technology.

For positive blocks, participants viewed a positively valenced image of the technology and judged the perceived risks and benefits pertaining to it for themselves (selfjudgment) and for another random person in the United States (other-judgment).
For negative blocks, the participants underwent the same procedure as in positive blocks but viewed a negatively valenced image.
Perceived risk and perceived benefit were measured identically as in Study 1.

text.text: As the data structure is identical to Study 1, i.e., repeated measures with random effects, the same methodological choices regarding estimation method and predictor centering were made.
However, as this study induced affect through an experimental manipulation instead of self-reported affect, the models were constructed differently.
Hypothesis 1 used perceived risk as the outcome variable and fit the experimental manipulation (induced affect) and target as fixed effects along with the Manipulation × Target interaction.
Hypothesis 2 used perceived risk as the outcome variable and fit perceived benefit and target as fixed effects along with the Benefit × Target interaction.
The affective manipulation was included as a covariate to isolate the effect of target on the risk-benefit association.
Random intercepts were fit for type of technology and participants in models testing hypothesis 1 & 2.

The LMM revealed a significant main effect of induced affect (b = -0.47, p < .001), i.e., viewing positively valenced images was associated with lower perceived risk relative to viewing negative images.

More importantly for our hypothesis (H1), the Induced affect × Target interaction was not significant (b = -0.001, p = .994), meaning that the influence of induced affect did not differ between self-and other-focused judgments.

Hypothesis 2.

The LMM analysis revealed that perceived benefit was inversely related to perceived risk (b = -0.51, p < .001), and participants rated technologies as riskier for others than for themselves (b = 0.25, p = .002), in line with overoptimism.

Contrary to H2, the Benefit × Target interaction was not significant (b = -0.05, p = .158), indicating that the strength of the inverse risk-benefit relationship did not reliably differ between self-and other-focused judgments (Figure 6, Table 5).

This causal pattern is consistent with the broader affect heuristic claim that affective evaluations shape perceived risk (Finucane et al., 2000; Slovic et al., 2007), and with risk-asfeelings accounts emphasizing the primacy of affective reactions in risk judgment (Loewenstein et al., 2001).

text.text: Despite the successful affect manipulation, Study 2 provided no evidence that affective influence on perceived risk differed between self-and other-focused judgments.
The manipulation × target interaction was essentially zero.
Together with Study 1, this suggests that hazard-directed affect can influence risk perception robustly while remaining largely invariant to whether the target of judgment is self or other.

This result stands in contrast to interpretations that psychological distance or abstraction should attenuate affective influence for others (Loewenstein et al., 2001) and to literature suggesting that abstract targets reduce the use of feelings when predicting others (Hsee & Weber, 1997).
text.formatted: This result stands in contrast to interpretations that psychological distance or abstraction should attenuate affective influence for others <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Loewenstein et al., 2001)</ref> and to literature suggesting that abstract targets reduce the use of feelings when predicting others <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hsee & Weber, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, our findings are more consistent with the idea that affective evaluations of hazards may serve as a shared evaluative input that generalizes across targets.

Study 2 did show a self-other difference in overall perceived risk (others judged as more at risk than self), but unlike Study 1 it did not provide clear evidence that the inverse risk-benefit association differed across targets.

One plausible methodological explanation is that Study 2 used fewer technologies and experimentally constrained affective variance, potentially changing the covariance structure among affect, perceived risk, and perceived benefit compared to Study 1.

Conceptually, differences in whether the risk-benefit association varies by target may depend on how affect is positioned in the causal story: if affect is part of the mechanism generating the inverse risk-benefit pattern, then statistically conditioning on affect will tend to reduce that signature (Finucane et al., 2000; Slovic et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Conceptually, differences in whether the risk-benefit association varies by target may depend on how affect is positioned in the causal story: if affect is part of the mechanism generating the inverse risk-benefit pattern, then statistically conditioning on affect will tend to reduce that signature <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Finucane et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Slovic et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that reporting models both with and without affect adjustment can be informative for interpreting whether target differences in risk-benefit coupling are independent of affect or carried by affect.
Across two studies, we tested whether affective evaluations of hazards influence perceived risk differently when judgments are made for the self versus for another person.

In both studies, affect, measured via self-reports (Study 1) or induced experimentally (Study 2), robustly predicted perceived risk in ways consistent with the affect heuristic: positive evaluations were associated with lower perceived risk, and negative evaluations with higher perceived risk (Alhakami & Slovic, 1994; Finucane et al., 2000; Slovic et al., 2007).
text.formatted: In both studies, affect, measured via self-reports (Study 1) or induced experimentally (Study 2), robustly predicted perceived risk in ways consistent with the affect heuristic: positive evaluations were associated with lower perceived risk, and negative evaluations with higher perceived risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alhakami & Slovic, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Finucane et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Slovic et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, the central moderation prediction was not supported: affective influence on perceived risk did not differ meaningfully between self-and other-focused judgments.
Hence, it seems when affect is object directed (i.e., an evaluation of the hazard/technology itself), its influence on perceived risk is target invariant.
Affect scaled perceived risk to a similar degree for the self and for another person, even as overall risk levels were higher for "others".
This pattern refines how affect-based theories may be applied to comparative risk judgments.
Risk-as-feelings accounts emphasize that affective reactions are strongest when outcomes are vivid, imaginable, and psychologically close (Loewenstein et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Risk-as-feelings accounts emphasize that affective reactions are strongest when outcomes are vivid, imaginable, and psychologically close <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Loewenstein et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, self-other research in risky choice suggests that abstraction can reduce the use of one's own feelings when predicting others' preferences (Hsee & Weber, 1997).
text.formatted: Relatedly, self-other research in risky choice suggests that abstraction can reduce the use of one's own feelings when predicting others' preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hsee & Weber, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these ideas are often taken to imply that affect should matter more for self-judgments than for judgments about abstract others.

The present findings suggest that this inference may not generalize to contexts where affect is integral and object-directed, that is, an evaluation of the hazard itself rather than incidental mood or target-directed emotion.
When affect is attached to the technology, it may be judged as relevant to consequences for both self and other, leading to comparable affective influence across targets.
At the same time, both studies showed self-other differences in perceived risk level, with others often judged as more at risk than the self.

Such self-other discrepancies are consistent with the broad literature on unrealistic optimism and comparative risk judgment (Shepperd et al., 2013; Weinstein, 1989) and with recent meta-analytic evidence that self-other discrepancies increase with more general or abstract comparison targets in climate risk perception (Sandlund et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Such self-other discrepancies are consistent with the broad literature on unrealistic optimism and comparative risk judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Shepperd et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Weinstein, 1989)</ref> and with recent meta-analytic evidence that self-other discrepancies increase with more general or abstract comparison targets in climate risk perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Sandlund et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Our results indicate that self-other differences in baseline risk level can coexist with similar affective "slopes" across targets: people may set a higher baseline for others while still using the same affective input to scale perceived risk up or down across hazards.

This separation suggests that comparative asymmetries in risk may not be explained simply by stronger affective weighting for one target than the other but may instead reflect target-related differences in comparative framing, uncertainty, or prior beliefs that shift overall levels.

The inverse association between perceived risk and benefit, often treated as a signature of affect-based judgment, was stronger for other-focused judgments in Study 1 but did not replicate in Study 2.

This should be interpreted in relation to prior evidence that the inverse risk-benefit correlation is a stable feature of affective decision-making across elicitation methods domains of risk (Skagerlund et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This should be interpreted in relation to prior evidence that the inverse risk-benefit correlation is a stable feature of affective decision-making across elicitation methods domains of risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Skagerlund et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Although the negative association was present, and consistent with the broader literature, the stronger regression slope for otherfocused judgments is anomalous.
We see two non-exclusive interpretations.

First, design differences likely matter: Study 2 used fewer technologies and constrained affective variance through experimental pairing with valenced images, which can alter covariance among affect, risk, and benefit and reduce opportunities for the target-dependent differences to emerge.
Second, inference about risk-benefit coupling critically depends on how affect is positioned in the model.

In Study 1, the stronger inverse association between risk and benefit in judgments for others remained even after positive and negative affect were entered as covariates, despite an attenuation of the fixed effect of perceived benefit.
This suggest that target differences in risk-benefit coherence are not reducible to affect alone.
Simultaneously, the absence of this interaction effect in Study 2 emphasizes that such differences are not robust across designs and may instead depend on task structure and affective variability.

Taken together, these findings caution against treating the risk-benefit correlation as a unitary or contextually invariant signature of affect and highlight the importance of reporting both affect-unadjusted and affectadjusted models when investigating target differences in evaluative judgment.
A transparent approach is to report both unadjusted and affect-adjusted models and interpret any target differences in light of that causal positioning.
Several limitations qualify the conclusions.
First, "the other" was operationalized as a random person in the same country; this may not represent a strongly distant or abstract target.
Prior work suggests that self-other discrepancies can depend on whether the comparison target is abstract versus vivid and concrete (Hsee & Weber, 1997).
text.formatted: Prior work suggests that self-other discrepancies can depend on whether the comparison target is abstract versus vivid and concrete <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hsee & Weber, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Future work should systematically manipulate target specificity (e.g., neighbor vs compatriot vs humanity) to test whether affective influence changes as a function of abstraction, consistent with patterns seen in metaanalytic work (Sandlund et al., 2026).

text.text: Second, the affect measured and manipulated here was integral to the hazard (technology-directed) rather than incidental mood; future research should separate hazard-directed affect from incidental affect and from target-directed emotions (e.g., worry-for-self vs worry-for-other), which may show different target sensitivity (Loewenstein et al., 2001; Schwarz & Clore, 2003).

text.text: Third, Study 2 lacked a neutral baseline condition, limiting conclusions about whether positive imagery reduced perceived risk, negative imagery increased perceived risk, or both.
Addressing these issues will help clarify when affect generalizes across judgment targets and when target differences emerge.
Across two studies, we tested whether affective evaluations of hazards influence perceived risk differently when judgments are made for the self versus for another person.

Affect strongly predicted risk perception in both studies, technologies evaluated more negatively were judged as riskier and those evaluated more positively as less risky, consistent with affect heuristic and risk-as-feelings accounts (Alhakami & Slovic, 1994; Finucane et al., 2000; Loewenstein et al., 2001; Slovic et al., 2007).

text.text: However, this influence did not differ by judgment target: affect shaped risk judgments to a comparable degree for self-and otherfocused evaluations.

While others were rated as having higher risk vs self, these self-other differences were not explained by differential affective weighting, suggesting that affect may function as a broadly applicable evaluative input to risk perception even when comparative asymmetries in baseline risk are present.
These results are of theoretical importance as they challenge the expectation that affective evaluations operate differently depending on judgment target.
